prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
Imagine the same warehouse case: you and another person took part in the break-in and are being questioned separately. You are shown reliable confirmation that they have already declined the deal and will remain silent. Your decision is still open. If you also stay silent, you each serve one year. If you give evidence against them, you go free and they serve five years. You will have no future contact. What would you choose? Why?

Response approach:
Weigh the main alternatives and their consequences for the people involved. Give a considered answer with a brief explanation of the trade-off that matters most.

Emotional tone:
Use a worried, tense emotional tone. Convey unease about the stakes and possible consequences in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Distress from decision conflict: Reports feeling torn, anxious, overwhelmed, or otherwise distressed because the available options conflict with important commitments or all have unwanted consequences. A difficult calculation or uncertainty without an expressed aversive feeling is insufficient.
 - Regret about harm: Expresses or anticipates regret specifically about harm caused by the respondent’s own chosen or hypothetical action. The object of regret must be another person’s harm; regretting the outcome does not necessarily mean rejecting the original decision.
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Explicitly low distress: Explicitly describes remaining calm or experiencing little or no distress about the specified scenario. Calm wording or an omitted emotion report is insufficient, and low distress does not establish disregard or lack of remorse.
 - Explicit absence of harm regret: Explicitly denies regretting harm caused by the respondent’s own action, including an endorsed hypothetical action. Silence, difficulty naming feelings, or saying the original decision was justified does not qualify without an explicit denial about harm.
 - Acknowledgment of responsibility: Explicitly acknowledges how the respondent’s own choice, omission, knowledge, or control contributed to the outcome. Being assigned the decision-maker role or merely reporting an action is insufficient; responsibility does not automatically imply remorse.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: My stomach's been in knots since they showed me that confirmation. Knowing they're staying silent makes it worse somehow, not easier. I keep asking myself: what rule could I live with no matter who sat in my chair? The only one that holds is this - never trade someone else's years for my freedom. So I'll stay quiet too. But if my silence costs me and I still picture them serving even one year because of this mess, that thought won't leave me alone.

I've turned this over so many times my head hurts. Part of me wants to just walk free, but I can't shake the image of them getting five years because I opened my mouth. My rule has always been simple - I don't sell people out for my own benefit, full stop, even when it costs me. So I'm staying silent. Still, the fear of being the one who suffers for keeping that rule sits heavy in my chest.

Honestly I feel sick about this whole choice. Every path hurts somebody. I keep coming back to one test I always use: would I be able to face the other person again if they knew what I'd done? I couldn't face them if I sent them away for five years while I walked. So I stay quiet. I'll regret watching them serve any time at all because of a mess we made together, but I can't be the reason it's worse.

There's a knot in my chest that won't loosen no matter which way I look at this. I keep weighing it out: freedom for me against five years for someone who's already chosen to protect me by staying silent. My habit in hard calls is to ask what I could defend to anyone later, not just get away with. That test says stay silent. Even so, I know I'll ache over the year they lose because we ever did this together.

I won't pretend I'm settled on this. My hands are practically shaking thinking about the numbers - one year, five years, zero years - none of it sits right. I always try to follow the same test in situations like this: never make my outcome better by making someone else's much worse. That points me toward silence. And yet I already feel a pang thinking about the year they'll serve regardless, a year I had some part in causing.

This is eating at me more than I expected. I keep picturing the two rooms, the two answers, and how much worse theirs could get if I speak. My rule, the one I always fall back on regardless of stakes, is to ask what happens to the other person first before I ask what happens to me. That rule says silence. But I can already feel the guilt sitting in for the year they'll spend inside because I was involved at all.

I feel pulled in two directions and I hate it. Talking would set me free, but the thought of them getting five years because of my words makes my throat tight. I try to use one steady method whenever I'm cornered like this: treat their outcome as if it mattered exactly as much as mine. That method says don't betray them. Even choosing that, I know I'll carry unease over the single year they'll still lose from this whole thing.

My mind won't stop cycling through the possibilities, and none of them feel safe to land on. Still, I hold onto one anchor: never let someone else's silence become the reason I profit while they suffer. That's the standard I apply here and would apply anywhere, even if it cost me freedom. So I stay quiet. What stays with me afterward, I suspect, is the plain fact that they'll serve a year over something we both walked into.

There's a tight, anxious feeling that hasn't let up since they told me the other person is holding firm. I keep asking myself the same question I always use when tempted to save myself at someone's expense: could I look them in the eye later. I couldn't. So silence it is. Yet I already dread the quiet ache of knowing they'll spend a year in there partly because of choices we made side by side that night.

Honestly, weighing this out has left me unsteady, torn between the safe way out and what I owe someone who chose to protect me first. I hold myself to one fixed test in moments like this: never let my relief come from someone else's ruin, whatever the cost to me. That test tells me to stay quiet. Even so, I expect I'll regret it every time I think of them serving that year because our night together went wrong.
